title: Descriptive Statistics
weightage: High — mean, median and "what happens if a value changes" appear on almost every test, often as Quantitative Comparison
intro: Descriptive statistics is the GRE's favourite way to test whether you actually understand a set of numbers or just know how to average them. Three measures of centre — mean, median and mode — plus the simplest measure of spread, the range, cover the bulk of what appears, and the test almost never asks for a raw calculation. Instead it asks what happens to the median when you add a value, whether the mean or the median is larger for a skewed set, or how to back out a missing number when the average is given. Because the on-screen calculator is basic, the winning approach is conceptual: know exactly what each measure is sensitive to, and you can answer most questions — especially Quantitative Comparison — without adding a single long column.

items.name: Median (odd n)
items.formula: the single middle value once sorted

items.name: Median (even n)
items.formula: average of the two middle values once sorted

items.name: Mode
items.formula: the value(s) that occur most often

topics.name: Mean, Median & Mode
topics.details: The three measures of centre answer three different questions. The mean is the balance point — add every value and divide by how many there are; it uses all the data, which is why a single extreme value drags it. The median is the positional middle: sort the list, then take the middle value (or the average of the two middle values if there is an even count); it ignores how far away the extremes are, so it is stable against outliers. The mode is simply the most frequent value, and a set can have one mode, several, or none. The single most useful GRE fact here is the relationship for skewed data: when a distribution has a long tail to the high side, the mean sits above the median; a long low tail pulls the mean below the median. Always sort before you touch the median — the most common error is reading the middle of the unsorted list.

solved.problem: Find the mean, median and mode of 4, 8, 8, 10, 15.
solved.solution: Already sorted. Mean = (4+8+8+10+15)/5 = 45/5 = 9. Median = middle value = 8. Mode = 8 (occurs twice). Note the mean (9) exceeds the median (8) because 15 pulls the tail right.

solved.problem: The median of 3, 7, x, 12, 18 (already sorted) is 9. Find x.
solved.solution: With 5 values the median is the 3rd, which is x. So x = 9. (Check the sort holds: 7 ≤ 9 ≤ 12, valid.)

solved.problem: A data set has 6 values: 2, 5, 5, 9, 11, 14. Find the median.
solved.solution: Even count, so average the 3rd and 4th values: (5 + 9)/2 = 7. The median need not be a value in the set.

solved.problem: Quantitative Comparison. List: 10, 12, 12, 20, 46. Quantity A: the mean. Quantity B: the median. Which is greater?
solved.solution: Mean = (10+12+12+20+46)/5 = 100/5 = 20. Median = middle value = 12. Quantity A (20) > Quantity B (12): the high outlier 46 lifts the mean but not the median. Answer: A is greater.

unsolved.problem: Find the mean of 12, 15, 21, 24, 28.
Find the median of 9, 3, 14, 7, 3, 20.
hints: Even count — average the two middle values.

unsolved.problem: Find the mode of 6, 9, 9, 11, 6, 9, 4.
hints: Count how often each value appears.

unsolved.problem: A set of 5 numbers has mean 14. Four of them are 10, 12, 16, 20. Find the fifth.
For 5, 8, 8, 40, is the mean greater than, less than, or equal to the median?
hints: Median of 4 values = average of 8 and 8.
unsolved.answer: Mean (15.25) is greater than the median (8)

topics.name: Range & Outliers
topics.details: The range is the crudest measure of spread: greatest value minus least value. Because it depends only on the two extreme numbers, it is extremely sensitive to outliers — values that sit far from the rest of the data. The GRE exploits this contrast constantly: an outlier can swing the range and the mean dramatically while leaving the median and the mode untouched. That is the whole reason the median is called "robust". When a question adds or removes a value, ask which statistics it can actually reach: a new value between the current minimum and maximum leaves the range unchanged, while a value outside that band expands it. A subtle point worth internalising — adding the same constant to every value shifts the mean and median by that constant but leaves the range and standard deviation completely unchanged, because spread does not care where the data sits, only how stretched out it is.

solved.problem: A set is 20, 22, 25, 28, 30. A value of 90 is added. What happens to the range and the median?
solved.solution: Range was 30 − 20 = 10; now 90 − 20 = 70, so it jumps by 60. Median was 25 (3rd of 5); with six values it is the average of 25 and 28 = 26.5. The outlier hammers the range but barely moves the median.

solved.problem: Every value in a data set is increased by 7. What happens to the mean and the range?
solved.solution: The mean increases by 7 (it shifts with the data). The range is unchanged: both the max and the min rose by 7, so their difference is identical.

solved.problem: Quantitative Comparison. Set S = {3, 4, 5, 6, 7}. Quantity A: the range of S. Quantity B: the range of S after each element is multiplied by 2. Which is greater?
solved.solution: Range of S = 7 − 3 = 4. After doubling, S = {6, 8, 10, 12, 14}, range = 14 − 6 = 8. Multiplying scales the range by the same factor. Quantity B (8) > Quantity A (4). Answer: B is greater.

unsolved.problem: Find the range of 45, 12, 67, 23, 8, 51.
A set has range 40 and minimum 12. What is its maximum?
To {10, 14, 18, 22} you add one value and the range stays 12. Give one value that works.
hints: Any new value must not fall outside 10–22.

unsolved.problem: Each value of a set is decreased by 5. The old range was 30. New range?
hints: Subtracting a constant shifts all values equally.

unsolved.problem: Set {2, 4, 6, 8, 100}: which changes more when 100 is removed, the mean or the median?
hints: Mean uses every value; the median is positional.
unsolved.answer: The mean changes far more (24 → 5) than the median (6 → 4)

topics.name: Weighted & Missing-Value Means
topics.details: A weighted mean applies when values do not all count equally — different group sizes, different credit hours, or different frequencies. You cannot simply average the sub-averages; you must weight each by its count: total of (weight × value), divided by the total weight. A classroom of 30 students averaging 70 combined with 20 students averaging 90 does not average to 80 — it is (30×70 + 20×90)/50 = 78, pulled toward the larger group. The mirror-image skill is the missing-value problem, which the GRE loves as Numeric Entry: if the target mean and the count are known, the required sum is fixed (sum = mean × n), so any single missing value is forced. Think in totals, not averages — nearly every "what must the sixth score be to average 85?" question collapses to one subtraction once you convert the target average into a required total.

solved.problem: A class of 30 averages 70 on a test; a class of 20 averages 90. What is the combined average?
solved.solution: Weighted mean = (30×70 + 20×90)/(30+20) = (2100 + 1800)/50 = 3900/50 = 78. It leans toward the larger (30-student) group.

solved.problem: A student scores 82, 88 and 91 on three exams weighted 20%, 30% and 50%. Find the weighted average.
Five numbers average 24. Four of them are 18, 22, 26 and 30. Find the fifth.
solved.solution: Required sum = 24 × 5 = 120. Known four sum to 96. Fifth = 120 − 96 = 24.

solved.problem: A shopper buys 3 kg of rice at $2/kg and 2 kg at $4.50/kg. What is the average price per kg?
solved.solution: Weight by quantity: (3×2 + 2×4.50)/(3+2) = (6 + 9)/5 = 15/5 = $3.00 per kg — not the simple average $3.25.

unsolved.problem: A team of 40 averages 60 and a team of 10 averages 85. Combined average?
Four numbers average 50. Three are 40, 55 and 65. Find the fourth.
Scores of 90 and 70 carry weights 3 and 1. Weighted mean?
A student has averaged 78 over 4 exams. What is needed on a 5th to raise the average to 80?
A 10-litre mix is 20% acid; a 5-litre mix is 50% acid. Overall acid percent when combined?
hints: Acid volume, not percent, is what adds.

topics.name: Effect of Changing a Data Point
topics.details: This is the single most GRE-characteristic idea in the whole chapter, and it rewards reasoning over computation. When you add, remove or alter one value in a set, each statistic responds differently, and knowing the pattern lets you answer without recomputing anything. The mean moves in the direction of the change, by (change in total)/(number of values) — so adding a value above the current mean raises it, and below it lowers it; adding a value exactly equal to the mean leaves it unchanged. The median often does not move at all, because a new value on one side of the middle may only shift the position slightly, or not at all. The mode changes only if the frequencies change. The classic Quantitative Comparison here gives you a set, changes one value, and asks you to compare the new mean or median with the old — the answer is usually reachable by pure logic. A powerful shortcut: adding a value equal to the current mean keeps the mean fixed but can still move the median, so "the mean is unchanged" never implies "the median is unchanged".

solved.problem: A set of 5 numbers has mean 20. A sixth number, 32, is added. Find the new mean.
solved.solution: Old sum = 20 × 5 = 100. New sum = 132 over 6 values. New mean = 132/6 = 22. The mean rose because 32 exceeds the old mean.

solved.problem: In the set 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 the value 12 is changed to 22. What happens to the mean and the median?
solved.solution: Median is the 3rd value, 8, and is untouched by changing the largest value. Mean was 8; the total rises by 10, so the new mean is 8 + 10/5 = 10. Mean up, median flat — the signature GRE contrast.

solved.problem: A list of 7 test scores has median 15. One score below the median is increased but stays below 15. Does the median change?
solved.solution: No. With 7 values the median is the 4th when sorted. Raising a value that remains below the middle does not change which value sits 4th, so the median stays 15.

solved.problem: Quantitative Comparison. Set has n values with mean m. A new value equal to m is added. Quantity A: the new mean. Quantity B: m. Which is greater?
solved.solution: New sum = nm + m = (n+1)m over (n+1) values, so new mean = m exactly. Adding a value equal to the mean never moves the mean. Quantity A = Quantity B. Answer: the two are equal.

unsolved.problem: A set of 4 numbers has mean 15. A fifth number, 25, is added. New mean?
In 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 the value 3 is replaced by 3. Does the mean change? By how much?
hints: Mean depends only on total and count.

unsolved.problem: A set of 6 numbers has mean 30. Removing one value leaves a mean of 32 over 5 values. Find the removed value.
To {2, 4, 6, 8} you add a number equal to the current mean. Give the new median.
A set of 5 numbers has mean 12. If each value is increased by 3, the new mean is?
hints: Adding 3 to every value adds 3 to the mean.
No need to recompute the total.

shortcuts: Convert a target average into a required TOTAL (sum = mean × n) before doing anything else — most "what score is needed" questions collapse to one subtraction.
Sort before you read the median. The commonest error is taking the middle of the unsorted list.
Adding or subtracting the same constant to every value shifts the mean and median by that constant but leaves the range and standard deviation unchanged.
A new value equal to the current mean leaves the mean fixed — a fast Quantitative Comparison shortcut.
For skewed data, the tail pulls the mean: a high outlier makes mean > median; a low outlier makes mean < median.
Weighted averages lean toward the group with the larger weight — never average the sub-averages directly.
Multiplying every value by k multiplies the mean, median AND range by k.
mistakes: Averaging two group averages directly instead of weighting them by group size.
Reading the median off an unsorted list.
Assuming a change to one value moves the median — often it moves the mean while the median stays put.
Thinking "the mean is unchanged" implies "the median is unchanged" (adding a value equal to the mean can still shift the median).
Forgetting that adding a constant to every value leaves the range and standard deviation unchanged.
Treating the range as robust — a single outlier can swing it wildly while the median barely moves.

pyq.q: Quantitative Comparison — Column A: the mean of 2, 4, 6, 8, 100. Column B: the median of the same set. Which is greater?
pyq.a: Column A. Mean = 120/5 = 24; median = 6. The outlier 100 lifts the mean far above the median.

pyq.q: Numeric Entry — A student has scored 84, 78 and 90. What must the fourth score be for an average of 85?
pyq.a: Required total = 85 × 4 = 340; scored so far 252; needed = 88.

pyq.q: Data Interpretation — A set of five values has mean 40. If one value of 60 is removed, what is the mean of the remaining four?
Multiple-answer — Which statistics are unchanged when 10 is added to every value of a data set? (range, mean, median, standard deviation)
pyq.a: Range and standard deviation. The mean and median each rise by 10; spread is unaffected.

flashcards.back: average of the two middle values (sorted)

flashcards.front: Add a constant c to every value
flashcards.back: mean and median rise by c; range and SD unchanged

flashcards.front: Add a value equal to the mean

flashcards.back: high-tail: mean > median; low-tail: mean < median

summary: Mean uses every value and is dragged by outliers; median is positional and robust; mode is the most frequent value.
Always sort before finding a median; for an even count, average the two middle values.
Range = max − min and is highly sensitive to a single outlier.
Weight sub-averages by their counts — never average averages directly.
Missing-value problems: convert the target mean into a required total, then subtract.
Changing one value shifts the mean by (change)/n but often leaves the median untouched.
Adding a constant to every value shifts centre but not spread; multiplying scales both.
Most GRE questions here — especially Quantitative Comparison — are reasoning, not calculation.
